subject: English
passage: Periods of sea-ice cover in the Arctic Ocean have been growing shorter as a result of climate changes, potentially enabling increased carbon dioxide (CO₂) absorption through greater productivity of ice-edge phytoplankton such as Phaeocystis pouchetii and other marine algae, but also potentially enabling increased CO₂ output through greater air-sea outgassing (CO₂ released as surface waters warm and lose their capacity to hold dissolved gas). Oceanographer Lwazi Hakim and his colleague Hiroshi Han developed a model incorporating numerous inputs—years of sea surface temperature and wind speed data among them—to evaluate the effects of climate changes on the CO₂ balance in the Arctic Ocean, concluding that net CO₂ is likely to increase if open-water conditions arrive earlier relative to the onset of spring phytoplankton blooms.
prompt: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: Relatively early open-water conditions reduce the availability of nutrients needed for the growth of phytoplankton species such as P. pouchetii and lower the rate of air-sea outgassing.
choices.B: The warming of exposed surface waters enables air-sea outgassing to continue during a period in which phytoplankton species such as P. pouchetii have not yet begun their spring bloom.
choices.C: The effect of sea surface temperature on the growth of phytoplankton and on the rate of air-sea outgassing is stronger during the period of open water than during the period of sea-ice cover.
choices.D: Open-water conditions tend to persist longer in regions of relatively low phytoplankton productivity and high air-sea outgassing than in regions of relatively high phytoplankton productivity and low outgassing.

explanation: Choice B is the best answer because it presents a finding that, if true, would support the researchers' conclusion that net CO₂ is likely to increase if open-water conditions arrive earlier relative to the onset of spring phytoplankton blooms. The text explains that shorter sea-ice periods in the Arctic could enable both increased CO₂ absorption through phytoplankton productivity and increased CO₂ output through air-sea outgassing as surface waters warm. A finding that warming exposed surface waters allow outgassing to continue during a period when phytoplankton such as P. pouchetii have not yet bloomed would directly support this conclusion: if outgassing releases CO₂ during a window when phytoplankton are not absorbing it, CO₂ output would exceed absorption, resulting in a net increase in CO₂.
